posts.text:
Which programming language is genuinely growing? I stopped trusting the usual rankings and built my own.

Most "most popular language" lists rest on one number: searches, or Stack Overflow questions. Stack Overflow questions are down 98.7% since 2019. Developers ask AI now, so those rankings mostly measure who switched first.

So I combined four signals for 17 languages, 2022 vs 2026: developers pushing code on GitHub, 82,138 Hacker News job posts, the Stack Overflow developer survey, and Google searches. All as shares, so a language only scores by pulling ahead of the others.

What the data says:

- Rust is up on every signal it has. Share of GitHub developers +71%, job posts 6.0% to 8.4%.
- TypeScript more than doubled its GitHub share and climbed from 9th to 3rd. It overtook JavaScript in job posts in 2023.
- Python's GitHub share grew by a third, and it is again the language most named in job posts (25%).
- Java's GitHub share fell 39% and its job-post share halved, even though 41% more developers pushed Java code. Still second in job ads in the UK, US and India. Losing share is not dying.

Two things surprised me. Google searches moved against every other signal. And the developer survey's gap between "want to use" and "use now" turned out to predict the next two years: in a 2017-2024 backtest it called the direction right 71% of the time. It now leans towards Rust and Go.

Full analysis, data, Python and R code, and a free checker for your country in the first comment.

Which language would you bet on for the next two years?

posts.title: [P] Detecting AI-written product reviews: 86% caught at 1% FPR on seen models, 29% to 37% on the newest unseen ones
posts.text:
I built a small detector for AI-written product reviews and tested it the way fake reviews actually arrive: from models it hasn't seen.

**Data.** Human Amazon reviews written before 2019 and GPT-2 fakes (Salminen et al. 2022), and reviews from nine chat models in the CRSD dataset, from Gemini 1.5 Flash to GPT-5.2 Instant. I matched 4,018 human and 4,018 AI reviews on sentiment and length (5-word bins) and normalised whitespace and quotes, so length and formatting can't do the work.

**Models.** TF-IDF word and character n-grams with logistic regression; gradient boosting on 24 style-only features; and a compact model that runs in the browser.

**Results (5-fold CV).**

- Full n-gram model: AUC 0.990, catches 86% of AI reviews at a 1% false-flag rate.
- Style only, no vocabulary: AUC 0.960.
- A detector trained on GPT-2 fakes catches 1% of the modern reviews (AUC 0.56).
- Leave-one-generator-out at 1% FPR: GPT-5.2 Instant 29%, GPT-5 mini 35%, Gemini 3 Flash 37%, the six older models 63% to 87%.

**Tells.** 70% of AI reviews open with "The" or "This", against 10% of human ones. 1% end without punctuation (human: 18%), and 1% contain a number (human: 12%).

**Limitations.** CRSD used generic prompts and its topics don't match the human set perfectly. The style-only model's 0.96 suggests topic isn't doing most of the work, but a generator set with varied prompts would be a better test. The human reviews are all pre-2019 Amazon.

Code (MIT): https://github.com/truthwithdata/analysis/tree/main/ai-written-review-detector

Write-up with a live demo: https://truthwithdata.com/case-studies/detecting-ai-written-reviews.html?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=2026-11-17-rd-ml-ai-reviews

I'd be interested in views on the right evaluation here. Leave-one-generator-out feels like the minimum, but it still assumes the next model resembles the last nine.

Stack Overflow had 19,801 new questions from January to October this year. In the same months of 2019 it had 1,474,916.

That is a 98.7% fall, and most of it came after ChatGPT launched in November 2022.

It matters beyond Stack Overflow. Many "most popular programming language" rankings are built on question counts or search volumes. When every language's questions and searches fall together, the ranking stops measuring how much a language is used. It measures which communities moved to AI assistants first. Google searches for programming languages fell too: 22% in the US, 32% in the UK and 52% in India over four years.

When I ranked 17 languages properly, by the code developers actually push and the jobs that ask for them, search interest moved in the opposite direction to every other signal.

If a ranking doesn't say what it measures, assume it measures attention, not use.

Same languages, different countries. How the share of developers writing each language on GitHub changed between mid-2022 and mid-2026:

UK: TypeScript +98%, Rust +60%, Python +24%. Java's GitHub share fell 39% while UK searches for it rose 24%. C# ranks last, down on all four signals.

posts.title: Which programming languages are actually growing in the UK? GitHub, job posts, the SO survey and searches, 2022 vs 2026
posts.text:
I get asked "which language should I learn?" a lot, and most rankings I could point people to are built on Stack Overflow questions or Google searches. Stack Overflow questions are down 98.7% since 2019, so I combined four signals instead for 17 languages, 2022 vs 2026: the share of developers pushing code on GitHub (GitHub Innovation Graph), Hacker News job posts, the Stack Overflow developer survey, and Google searches.

For the UK:

- TypeScript's share of GitHub developers is up 98%, Rust's 60%, Python's 24%.
- Java's GitHub share fell 39% while UK searches for it rose 24%. Searches often moved the opposite way to the other signals.
- C# ranks last in the UK, losing share on all four signals.
- On 5 November, UK IT job ads named Python most often (8,071), then Java (3,125), JavaScript (2,216), C# (2,003) and TypeScript (1,987). Rust (468 ads) and Go had the highest mean advertised salaries, about £94,400 and £89,800.

Losing share isn't dying: Java and C# are still near the top of UK job ads by volume. If you need a job soon, volume matters more than momentum.

Caveats: the job-ad counts are one day's snapshot from Adzuna; Hacker News posts lean towards US startups; GitHub shares count developer-language pairs, not hours of work.

For people hiring in the UK: does this match what you see? C# coming last on momentum surprised me, given how much .NET work there is.

Full method, data and code, plus a checker you can set to the UK: https://truthwithdata.com/blog/which-programming-language-is-genuinely-growing.html?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=2026-11-19-rd-cscquk-langs
